newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK rates on hold as focus shifts to taxes.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK rates on hold as focus shifts to taxes.

text.p: UK base rates will stay on hold this year as government focus shifts from monetary to fiscal policy ahead of the general election due by May 1997, a Reuters survey of analysts showed on Friday.

The poll of forecasts from 20 banks -- carried out after Thursday's confirmation that rates were left on hold at this month's monetary meeting -- showed a majority of 13 economists expect UK base rates to stay on hold at 5.75 percent this year.
But by the end of June next year, base rates are forecast to rise to six or 6.25 percent.

On the fiscal side, the mean of forecasts showed analysts expect a net tax giveaway of 2.80 billion sterling in the budget, which Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke is to present on November 26.

"Rates will be on hold until after the election. Next year they will have to rise because the economy will be growing pretty fast by then and the labour market will be tighter," said Ian Amstad, senior European economist at Bankers Trust.
He expects base rates to remain at 5.75 percent this year, rising to 6.25 percent by next June.
Chief economist at IBJ International Steven Hannah said, "There is more political advantage in tax cuts". He forecast the net tax giveaway will be three billion sterling.
But six contributors to the survey still expect a base rate cut to 5.50 percent before the end of this year.
Steven Lewis, director at London Bond Broking Company, forecasts the Chancellor will slice off 25 basis points.
He expects the cut to be made later this month, after the next monetary meeting on September 23 and before the ruling Conservative Party conference which starts on October 8.
But Lewis also forecasts a quick reversal, with base rates back up to six percent by the middle of 1997.

Only one economist forecast higher base rates at the end of this year. Richard Jeffrey, group economist at Charterhouse, believes Chancellor Clarke will be forced to raise rates to 6.25 percent by December.
"They (Conservative government) will want to be seen as being risk-averse. The last thing they will want is pressure to raise rates emerging in the last month or so before the election."
Along with David Smith, economist at Williams de Broe, Jeffrey expects expects base rates at 6.75 percent by mid-1997.
Sixteen economists forecast higher base rates by the end of next June. They said price pressures resulting from healthy economic growth will force the issue.
According to Philip Uglow, economist at Union Discount, there is already evidence of a strong pick-up in the economy.
"Growth is being fuelled by consumer spending and will continue into next year."
With mortage rates at historically low levels, analysts mostly agree the advantages of cutting rates are limited.
But to be seen as being prudent, the expected tax reductions will be matched by what should appear to be equivalent cuts in expenditure, they say.
"I would expect the cuts to be dressed up in a neutral budget," said Adrian Owens, European Economist at Julius Baer Investments.
